books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text:
“...That there is hereby established in the War Department, to continue during the present war of rebellion, and for one year thereafter, a Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, to which shall be committed, as hereinafter provided, the supervision and management of all abandoned lands, and the control of all subjects relating to refugees and freedmen from rebel States. . . . The Secretary of War may direct such issues of provisions, clothing, and fuel as he may deem needful for the immediate and temporary shelter and supply of destitute and suffering refugees and freedmen, and their wives and children. . . .”

—Freedmen’s Bureau Act, March 3, 1865
stimulus.source_note: Freedmen’s Bureau Act, March 3, 1865 (13 Stat. 507). Public domain. Wording verified against the act text in the Congressional Serial Set (govinfo). Ellipses mark omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The act says the Bureau would last “during the present war of rebellion, and for one year thereafter,” and would give “immediate and temporary” relief. Those time limits best show that

options.text: Congress planned the Bureau as a permanent department.
options.misconception: Background: a one-year limit after the war is the opposite of a permanent department.

options.text: the Bureau was meant to replace state governments forever and run the South.
options.misconception: Background: the Bureau was a relief agency, not a replacement for state government.

options.text: Southern planters asked for the Bureau’s help.
options.misconception: Background: planters opposed the Bureau, which helped their former workers bargain.

options.text: even its supporters saw the aid as a short-term bridge, not a permanent program.

rationales.A: Background: a one-year limit after the war is the opposite of a permanent department.
rationales.B: Background: the Bureau was a relief agency, not a replacement for state government.
rationales.C: Background: planters opposed the Bureau, which helped their former workers bargain.
rationales.D: Every time limit in the act points the same way: “during the present war,” “one year thereafter,” “immediate and temporary.” Even the Bureau’s friends in Congress imagined a short bridge to self-reliance, not a lasting federal presence.
rationales.general:
1. Read the time words: “during the present war,” “one year thereafter,” “immediate and temporary.”
2. Each one puts an end date on the help.
3. Background: Congress later extended the Bureau, but the original act shows how short its makers expected the job to be.
4. That short horizon is part of why the Bureau’s work stayed unfinished.
Remember: time limits in a law tell you how long its makers thought the problem would last.
